summary:
Outpost Cadet is a junior astronaut mission trainer made of three browser games that teach how a real Moon or Mars outpost survives. In the solo game, students command a four-person crew for 30 days, landing on the surface and then balancing power, food, life support and radiation shielding while handling solar storms, dust storms and equipment failures. Signal Lost is a multiplayer social-deduction game where a crew repairs a station while a hidden saboteur works against them. Crew Rush has four players take the roles of Engineer, Commander, Botanist and Geologist and keep the base running through one working day.

It meets the challenge by turning the four core systems into decisions where every choice has a cost and no option is free. Real NASA data runs through it, including live space weather, measured radiation doses, Moon and Mars maps, and Earth-to-Mars communication delay.

It matters because kids learn space science best by doing it. Playing teaches them trade-offs, teamwork and why every resource counts when help is minutes or months away.
details:
What it does and how it works. Outpost Cadet is a family of three browser games that teach kids aged 7 to 12 how a Moon or Mars outpost survives. In the solo game, players land a craft with a powered-descent mini-game that uses real gravity (1.62 m/s² on the Moon, 3.71 on Mars). They then spend 30 days assigning crew tasks while managing power, food, life support and radiation shielding, and they face random events such as solar storms, dust storms and scrubber failures. Signal Lost is a multiplayer social-deduction game with 18 NASA-based tasks and a five-chapter story, in which a hidden saboteur AI works against the crew. Crew Rush is a four-player co-op game where each player takes a role (Engineer, Commander, Botanist or Geologist) and keeps the base running through one working day.

Benefits and intended impact. Players learn the real trade-offs of space missions by living them. Every option costs something, and a test checks that no decision is free. Terms like radiation dose, ISRU and light-time delay are explained in context. Because it runs in a browser on phones, tablets and computers, it works in a classroom or at home. The solo game needs no install, server or internet. The goal is to build interest in space science and systems thinking in young learners.

Tools and technology. Everything is vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with canvas graphics. The multiplayer games run on a hand-written Node.js (18+) HTTP and WebSocket server with no dependencies. Phones join by scanning a QR code. We tested with Node’s built-in test runner, including 10 simulation tests and full multiplayer playthroughs with scripted players. A balance script played 2,400 bot missions to tune difficulty. Real data comes from NASA DONKI, OSDR RadLab, Moon Trek and Mars Trek, JPL orbit data and the Canadian Space Agency, with NOAA as a fallback.

Creativity. We turned systems engineering into three different play styles: solo strategy, social deduction and role-based co-op. In Crew Rush, “Ask Mission Control” simulates real communication delay, so on Mars the answer arrives after the crew has had to decide. Each number is labeled LIVE or SAVED, so saved data is never passed off as live.

Factors we considered. We aimed at ages 7 to 12 with plain-language explanations. We kept setup simple, with no install and the same Wi-Fi only. We checked difficulty with bot testing so a sensible plan wins and a careless one loses. We also documented our simplifications honestly. For example, oxygen output is scaled up from what MOXIE achieved, and health is a single number.
